comments.text:
Overview: 

The scan() function, used by the read functions and others, only allows a single byte as separator (sep).  While this is fine for simple datasets, it's problematic for complex data sets such as those that might contain lengthy comments, byte dumps, embedded newlines, and so on.

It would be very helpful to be able to specify a multi-character separator.

Steps to Reproduce: (Borrowed from the documentation for base::scan())

sep: by default, scan expects to read ‘white-space’ delimited input fields. Alternatively, sep can be used to specify a character which delimits fields. A field is always delimited by an end-of-line marker unless it is quoted.  If specified this should be the empty character string (the default) or NULL or a character string containing just one single-byte character.


Actual Results: Only a single separator character can be used.

Expected (desired) Results: Multiple separator characters can be used.  This is particularly important for cases where text files with arbitrary characters, possibly with unmatched quotes (of any type) are being parsed.  The only way to handle such files is to create a ridiculously long separator that is not likely to show up in the dataset, such as sep='|%$!?MYSEPARATOR?!$%|', and work with that.  Incidentally, the write functions allow multi-character separators, but their read counterparts do not (because of the scan() limitation).

Build Date & Hardware & Additional Builds and Platforms: All (Base).

Additional Information:  

This issue has been challenging for many R users who are working on data with either nonstandard separators or arbitrary character content.  In the case of nonstandard separators, most of them have resorted to pre-processing outside of R, which is a shame.  However, in the case of arbitrary character content parsing, external parsing doesn't resolve the issue, since reading back into R simply recreates the issue.  Further, stringsplit()/readLines() based solutions are fine except for the parsing of data with embedded newlines, which also becomes a problem.  The ability to set an arbitrary separator with write() already exists to address this issue.  We just need the ability to read arbitrary separators as a counterpart.

Here are some of the threads that I found while searching for solutions to this issue.  Note that none of them address the arbitrary data parsing cases with embedded newlines:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/18186357/importing-csv-file-with-multiple-character-separator-to-r

http://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/multiple-separators-in-sep-argument-for-read-table-td856567.html

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/7883859/how-to-read-a-text-file-into-gnu-r-with-a-multiple-byte-separator

https://www.mail-archive.com/r-help@r-project.org/msg18035.html

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2732397/why-the-field-separator-character-must-be-only-one-byte

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17223844/one-byte-separator-argument-in-read-table

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/29740992/r-invalid-sep-value-must-be-one-byte

comments.text:
Making this change is harder than it looks, unfortunately, and so I think this is unlikely to happen. I suspect the simplest change here would be to recommend an alternate tool for when one wants to read data using multi-byte separators, or to perform some amount of preprocessing and perhaps post-processing to transform separators into a single byte.

Some more analysis below.

---

  The relevant code is src/main/scan.c. The inner reader (fillBuffer, lines
  ~397-456) consumes one byte at a time and tests it against a single int
  sepchar, with exactly one byte of pushback (LocalData.save, unscanchar at
  line 231). Allowing a multi-byte separator changes several things at once:

  1. Look-ahead and rollback. On seeing the first byte of sep, we have to
     read up to N-1 more bytes and either commit (it was the separator) or
     back out, copying the consumed prefix into the field. The existing
     1-byte pushback isn't enough.

  2. CSV-style quoting. The current code peeks one byte after a closing
     quote to decide "is this the separator or end-of-line?" That peek
     becomes a multi-byte compare with the same rollback issue.

  3. DBCS locales. The reader is byte-oriented but treats DBCS lead/trail
     bytes specially. A multi-byte separator must not be allowed to straddle
     a character boundary, which adds another validity check.

  4. strip.white interactions. A separator like " | " or "\t|\t" makes the
     trim rules ambiguous and needs documented precedence.

  5. Embedded newlines. This is the bigger issue for the use case you
     describe. scan() unconditionally treats \n, \r, and EOF as record
     terminators (see lines 398-399). Even with a multi-byte field
     separator, an embedded newline still breaks the record. So multi-byte
     sep alone wouldn't actually solve the "arbitrary character content"
     problem you mention -- it solves the collision problem, but not the
     embedded-newline problem.

  None of this is unfixable, but it's a delicate change in a hot,
  locale-sensitive path, with a wide test surface across scan/read.table/
  read.csv. The bar to land it is high.


  Alternatives
  ------------

  For the "delimiter unlikely to collide with data" case, the canonical
  solution is a single-byte ASCII control character. C0 0x1E (Record
  Separator) and 0x1F (Unit Separator) were reserved by ASCII for exactly
  this purpose and never appear in well-formed text:

      sep = "\x1f"   # Unit Separator: between fields
                     # \x1e Record Separator: between records

  This works with current scan() and is strictly stronger than a long
  sentinel string, because the byte is by construction absent from text
  payloads.

  If the data already arrives with a multi-byte separator and you can't
  change the producer, substitute before parsing:

      raw <- readChar(path, file.info(path)$size, useBytes = TRUE)
      raw <- gsub("|%$!?MYSEP?!$%|", "\x1f", raw,
                  fixed = TRUE, useBytes = TRUE)

  Reading the whole file in one shot (rather than line-at-a-time) avoids
  the issue that readLines()-based approaches have with embedded newlines.

  If your fields can also contain literal \n characters that should not
  terminate a record, you'll need to substitute those too (e.g. to \x1e)
  before handing to scan().
